parsed.summary: The Lean theorem proves the intermediate value theorem on a closed interval. Let α be a densely ordered, conditionally complete linear order with the order topology, and δ a linear order with an order-closed topology. If f : α → δ is continuous on [a,b] with a ≤ b, then every y with f(a) ≤ y ≤ f(b) is attained at some point of [a,b]. Specializing α = δ = ℝ recovers the paper's statement exactly, so the Lean statement is a faithful generalization. There is no substantive caveat.

glossary.plain: For a ≤ b and f continuous on [a,b], the interval [f(a), f(b)] is contained in the image f([a,b]).
glossary.note: Stated in Mathlib's generality: a dense conditionally complete linear order maps into an order-closed linear order. ℝ → ℝ is a special case.

lean_claims.plain: Assume the following: α is a conditionally complete, densely ordered linear order with the order topology; δ is a linear order with an order-closed topology; a ≤ b in α; and f : α → δ is continuous on Icc a b. Then for every y with f a ≤ y ≤ f b there exists c ∈ [a,b] with f c = y.

paper_claims.plain: If f : [a,b] → ℝ is continuous and a ≤ b, then for every y with f(a) ≤ y ≤ f(b) there is c ∈ [a,b] with f(c) = y.

coverage.why: Lean allows general ordered domain and codomain types. ℝ satisfies all the typeclass assumptions, and set inclusion into the image is exactly the existence claim. Continuity only on Icc a b corresponds to f being defined on [a,b].

flags.explanation: Lean is more general than the paper because it uses abstract ordered types instead of ℝ. This is harmless; the paper's case follows by instantiation with α = δ = ℝ.
flags.probe_idea: example {a b : ℝ} (hab : a ≤ b) {f : ℝ → ℝ} (hf : ContinuousOn f (Set.Icc a b)) : Set.Icc (f a) (f b) ⊆ f '' Set.Icc a b := stmt hab hf
